description: Flame in Freefall uses Super Intelligence (AI) to analyze NASA's microgravity combustion data for spacecraft fire safety. Without gravity, flames become spherical, produce larger soot aggregates, and form invisible "cool flames" that evade standard sensors. Machine learning models predict ignition limits and airflow risks, enhancing real-time life support systems to protect deep-space missions.
summary:
Flames in Free Fall is an interactive educational website about fire safety, based on research into combustion in microgravity. It is written in TypeScript and compiled to JavaScript  and delivered as a single HTML page. Visitors can change gravity, oxygen level and airflow and watch a live flame simulation turn from an Earth-like teardrop into a blue sphere, or go out.

A flammability map, a scale calculator and a drop-tower simulator explain why weightlessness changes how fire behaves. The sections cover NASA experiments (Saffire, FLEX, ACME, SoFIE), recent findings on smoke and partial gravity, cabin atmospheres from the ISS to Apollo 1, a fire-risk assessment form, a response protocol and "flame balls", the leanest known fire.

The design uses a space-themed palette, an animated starfield and smooth transitions. A 28-second demo video shows the site in action. All curves, temperatures and indices are illustrative, not official NASA data.
details:
Flames in Free Fall is an interactive educational website about fire safety in microgravity. On Earth, buoyancy-driven convection shapes a flame into a yellow teardrop. In free fall that convection disappears, and the flame becomes a blue sphere that can die in conditions where an Earth flame would survive.

Visitors control gravity, oxygen level and airflow in a live canvas simulation and see the flame change shape, colour and stability. Around it, the site explains the physics:

  • Flammability map. Click or drag to place a point and see whether a flame would burn.
  • Scale calculator. A Péclet-number estimate shows when diffusion replaces convection.
  • Drop-tower simulator. Capsule motion follows s = gt²/2.
  • Cabin-atmosphere comparison. ISS, an exploration cabin and Apollo 1 side by side.
  • Fire-risk assessment form and response protocol.
  • Flame balls. A simulation of the leanest known fire, observed in NASA’s SOFBALL experiment.

A “New findings” section summarises recent research on scale effects, smoke behaviour and partial gravity.

Benefits

  • It runs in any browser, with no installation, account or server.
  • Visitors learn by experimenting rather than reading.
  • It is self-contained, so it can be hosted on any static host, and it sends no user data anywhere.
  • It includes keyboard focus styles, ARIA labels and reduced-motion support.

Expected impact

The project aims to make microgravity combustion research understandable to students, teachers and the public, and to show why fire safety must be rethought for orbital stations, the Moon and Mars, including hydrogen-fuelled spacecraft. Because it is a single shareable page, it can be used in classrooms, outreach events and science-communication projects.

Tools, languages and technology

  • Languages: TypeScript (compiled to JavaScript), HTML5, CSS3, SVG.
  • Graphics: HTML Canvas 2D (particle flame, map, flame balls, starfield) and inline SVG illustrations.
  • Build tools: TypeScript compiler, esbuild, html-minifier-terser (Node.js and npm).
  • Demo video: Python, Playwright with headless Chromium, and ffmpeg, rendering frames deterministically.
  • Fonts: Unbounded and Manrope.
  • Hardware: an ordinary computer and cloud Linux containers. No special hardware is needed to run the site.
  • AI assistance: the project was developed with the AI assistant Claude (Anthropic), which wrote and refined the code and content with the author. Check your competition’s rules on AI-assisted work and disclose accordingly.

Creativity

Instead of a static report, the project turns research data into play: a flame that morphs as you drag a slider, a capsule you drop yourself, flame balls you nudge with a “thruster”, and a mission-control look with a live starfield and a curved Earth horizon. Every illustration is drawn in code, so there are no external images.

Factors considered

  • Scientific accuracy: content is based on open sources, including NASA’s Technical Reports Server, NASA’s 2026 microgravity-fire article, NIST/NASA smoke research, and SOFBALL publications. Curves, temperatures and indices are illustrative, not certified data.
  • Honest scope: it is not an official NASA product and does not use NASA logos.
  • Performance and compatibility: a lightweight single file that works on desktop and mobile.
  • Accessibility and usability: responsive layout, readable contrast and motion that respects user settings.
  • Privacy: forms process data only in the browser.
  • Maintainability: typed TypeScript source with a simple build and an easy two-file or one-file deployment.
